newsitem.title: UK: TENNIS-STAWBERRIES SUFFER ON RAIN-RUINED AFTERNOON.
newsitem.headline: TENNIS-STAWBERRIES SUFFER ON RAIN-RUINED AFTERNOON.

text.p: Patiently arrayed in orderly rows, sheltering from the rain sweeping from the west on another rain-ruined afternoon at Wimbledon.
And not only the strawberries suffered on Thursday.
"Humid air moisture will not readily dry up," said the daily release from the London Weather Centre.
Which freely translated meant continuous, heavy rain falling impartially on the just, the unjust and 18 tennis courts in south-west London.
It can be happily reported that not all was gloom and doom.

The Champagne and Pimms tent had its first customer 75 minutes before play was due to begin on Centre Court. By mid-afternoon, some dedicated tipplers were soaked outwardly and inwardly in approximate equilibrium.

The ritual jibes about the price of strawberries and cream were both unfair and untrue. At 1.85 pounds ($3) they were not only cheaper than a slice of pepperoni pizza at the adjoining stall but also warmer.

Street vendors hawking brightly-coloured golf umbrellas reported impressive sales. Taxis shuttled to and from Southfields Station to the Number Five gate in an unending procession. Radio Wimbledon played Handel's Water Music.

The entrepreneurial instinct flourished. As a selling point, the mystifyingly named "Croquet Cafe" announced it had "undercover seating". In case anybody missed the point, the sign added three exclamation marks.
The press bar, already doing an encouraging trade, was crammed to over-flowing with intrepid news-hounds after reports that Mary Pierce and Mary Joe Fernandez would be distributing strawberries.
And still the rain came down.
At intervals a disembodied voice on the public address system updated spectators on the latest weather forecast, adding an English top-spin of his own.
"Not, I'm afraid, very encouraging," said the phantom voice.
The Royal Box was to feature Bird, Mr Dickie alongside the Earl and Countess of Harewood and the ambassadors of Kuwait and the Philippines.

Harold "Dickie" Bird, England's best-known cricket umpire until his retirement from the international list last year, was haunted by bad weather, breaking out in a nervous twitch at the hint of moisture in the air.
A possible counter to English mid-summer weather was suggested in a letter to the Times of London on Thursday.

"Would it not be appropriate, given the uncertainty as to what should be exhibited beneath the Millennium Dome (at Greenwich) if it were instead to be positioned over Wimbledon?," wrote reader G. Sreenan. "Surely this would prevent, in perpetuity, two notorious British washouts."
